titleStmt.title: Interview with Robert M. McMillan, March 26, 2004
titleStmt.author: Thomas A. Swope

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Robert M. McMillan was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran Robert M. McMillan. Mr. McMillan served in the U.S. Army with the 69th Division, 271st Regiment, Company I. He served in the European Theater and his highest rank was sergeant. I'm Tom Swope and this interview was recorded at Mr. McMillan's home in Stowe, Ohio on March 26th, 2004. Robert was 79 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: I was in Ellendale, North Dakota and when the Japanese bombed Pearl Harbor I was in high school.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of that day?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Oh, yes. It was a Sunday, of course, and we went to church and I had a friend whose parents ran a restaurant down in huge Ellendale, their downtown area. So after we had gone home and had a little lunch, why I went down to see my buddy about 1 o'clock in the afternoon and I walked into the restaurant and I says, well, did you hear? He said, hear what? That the Japanese had bombed Pearl Harbor. So I immediately turned around went home and told my folks about it and my -- couple of my buddies and I that evening went to the movies and oh, saw a film. I can't remember the name of it any more, but anyway, they were ferrying airplanes to Great Britain and the climatic scene was the hero, of course, crashed into the German Messerschmitt that was going to shoot them all down and save the day and as we came out they had a special edition of the Aberdeen. Aberdeen, South Dakota is the nearest really large town. Aberdeen American News had an extra out with what little was known about Pearl Harbor at that time and I still have a copy of the paper.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: If I'm not mistaken I think I know what movie that you are talking about. It might be called Captain of the Clouds.

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: That's right. It was.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: I just saw that one.

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: It was. It was.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Now were you and your classmates tempted to go out there and sign up the next day?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Not really. I mean I was -- I wasn't 17 at that time. I was -- my birthday was in December. I was December 18th. So I wasn't 17 at that time. And I figured that I would be lots better off if I finished high school as far as getting anywhere in the Army. Of course, I was going to be an officer. So I tried to sign up for all of the programs that were available. The Navy V-5 program and the V-12 program and so on and for one reason or another I didn't qualify. I didn't pass the eye test for the V-5 program I guess it was, which they gave the eye test in a room with illumination about like we have here which is very poor. And then I -- they said I had high blood pressure and I guess I had because I still have it today that I'm treating, but I didn't get into any of those programs. But they did give a test sponsored by the Army for the Army Specialized Training Program and when I -- I completed almost a year of college before I was 18. At that time they were drafting people. You couldn't volunteer any more. Everybody got drafted at that time and so they -- I evidently did well on the test since they sent me a card and said when you are inducted, why take this card along and show it to them. So I took the card along and when I was inducted, why I showed them the card and so I was sent to Camp Roberts, California and as a part of a rather unusual unit there. This was an infantry basic training facility and they had a company that was made up entirely of people that had been selected for the ASTP, the Army Specialized Training Program and we were kind of a shock to the cadre out there. They had been used to a little bit different type of people that they got in. They said they didn't know whether they liked us or not. You only had to tell these people things once and they understood it, but they were a little bit too much asking why are we doing this rather than just doing it. But I got about halfway through basic training and they brought in another group. So I got to start all over again and so I didn't -- I got out there in June and I didn't actually finish basic training until November because of the second group coming in and starting the entire process 17 weeks basic over again.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: June of '43?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: '43, right?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Yeah, June of '43.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: When you first went into the Army, was it a tough adjustment to be there with guys from all over the country?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Not really. I mean we got along very well. I mean we had, oh, we had a wide variety of backgrounds, but the group that I was with was probably more homogeneous than a lot of training groups were. In that all of the, essentially all the people in there had probably had at least one year of college or part of a year of college and so you don't -- didn't get quite the diversity that I ran into when I actually went into the 69th Division. There was a much wider range of backgrounds and abilities in the people that I met there than there was in the training unit. But we finally finished training and took a whole bunch of tests and then they shipped us off to various colleges all over the United States. I ended up at Syracuse University and I was there from November until March when they closed out the program. We were supposed to get a five year engineering degree in either three or four years. So they were really moving us along, but at that time they decided the war wasn't going to last that long and they need infantry lots worse than they needed engineering officers. So we got to go to various units and I went to the 69th Division. I was figuring out I got there on March 21st, 1944, just 60 years ago. So I just about 60 years ago that I got into the 69th Division, which was in Camp Shelby, Mississippi doing training there.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: How did the guys treat you when the ASKB guys came to Camp Shelby?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Most of them are pretty good. Our first sergeant greeted us a bunch of damn college professors. He was a World War I veteran and just had over 30 years of service, part of which was bad time because he struck an officer during World War I. So we spent a little time in the stockade, but he was our first sergeant, but he was all right. But I think that they were a little, I shouldn't say suspicious of us, but they -- think they found that we worked out pretty well. Quite a number of the people that came in from the SGP ended up as being noncommissioned officers as I finally did. So we got along all right. And I was assigned to a -- in one of the rifle squads second platoon and I was -- ended up as an assistant BAR man at that time, excuse me. So I got to carry the BAR part of the time and a little bit later on why they were looking for people that wanted to volunteer for the weapons platoon which is the 60 millimeter mortars and light machine guns. And so I figured, well, it is not real healthy to be BAR man or an assistant BAR man and that mortar isn't much heavier than the BAR. So I think I will volunteer to go to the weapons platoon. So I transferred to the weapons platoon and we trained in Mississippi and we, the division just before I came in had just finished up a series of maneuvers against the 442nd Regimental Combat Team, the Japanese group that went to Italy and did so well. And they were -- all I heard was griping that 442nd got to ride in trucks and we had to walk everyplace and that's why they did better than we did, which I don't know it was necessarily true, but at least that's what I heard at the time. And so we -- they would send out people as replacements in the division. Since it starting in 1943 had been primarily training replacements, a lot of which I understand went to the South Pacific, but we started a series, started at the company level and working up through division maneuvers. And so we went through this. We were out in the field on D-Day and this was announced to us out in the field that they had invaded the coast of France and so we knew that probably we would end up there, although we weren't sure sooner or later, but we finished our division series maneuvers and at the end of October and it was we got on our troop trains and were to go to Camp Kilmer, New York. I remember it was October 31st because it was Halloween and all along the railroad tracks you could see the jack-o-lanterns and so on in the little towns that we went through. And so we got up to Camp Kilmer and were there, actually we were there I got -- we got a 48 hour pass while we were at Camp Kilmer and I went up to New York and was in the Times Square on election day in 1944. Yeah, so I got to see that and then I went down to Washington D.C. and saw some of the Smithsonian, a little bit of that and then headed back to Camp Kilmer and then we finally shipped out the end of November and got over to England. Well, I think that was around the first of December, something like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What was the crossing like?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Really it wasn't too bad. We were on what had been a passenger liner. I think it was originally German made and seized and converted to a troop carrier and we were in a good place. We were up on what had been one of the promenade decks, which were enclosed, although our bunks were 17, not 17 high, about six high, something like that, with a few inches between them, but we were in a good -- I was in the good part of the vessel and also, I was very fortunate at that particular time. The squadron, the motor squadron I was in had a gunner that had not gone overseas because he was too old to go overseas. He had been one of the original men so they said he was too old to go overseas. And so I was an acting sergeant as the mortar squad leader and since I was not a real sergeant they couldn't put me in charge of detail to do things. And since I was acting sergeant, I really shouldn't go on details to do things for other people. So for at least three days I got to lie on my spacious bed and be seasick, but after about three days I got over that and from there on it was quite nice, but the crossing itself was not that bad. The weather was fairly good. As far as I know we did not encounter any submarines or things of that nature and it was a fairly good crossing. It took 15 days it took us to get over there. I think is not too bad and we came in south, landed at Southampton and we went to Winchester and we were in Winchester Barracks, which was, of course, an Army thing, which was quite a different. Their heating was by fireplace. In the room they had a little stove kind of and you were supposed to heat with coal. Well, I don't know how you start it nor did anybody else in our unit and we spent a lot of kindling and time trying to get the coal to burn in the fireplace and never succeeded and it was pretty cold. It was in December in England and pretty cold there. So we were pretty cold in Winchester Barracks. Also, they had -- all the plumbing had been added after the barracks was originally was built, so all the plumbing was gone. All the pipes were on the outside of the building rather than inside, which was different. They then moved us out into the country and we were in the mission huts out there near what had been a country manor of some Englishman they had commandeered and then the officers were in that building. We had barracks and we had showers and we'd have hot water sometimes to wash with. We did not have flush toilets. We had somebody come around and collected things every day or two and it was fertilizer, I'm sure, and it was very livable. And so we spent our time there and then I think the 69th Division is probably the only unit I have ever heard of that lost half of its fighting capacity in one day without being in combat. Because on Christmas day of 1944, half of the Division was taken as replacements for the Battle of the Bulge. So we were -- had come overseas as a very well-trained unit who were familiar with all of the people in our units and their capabilities and their shortcomings as well and Christmas day half of them were gone and we were no longer any type of a fighting unit at all. So we remained in England until January, middle of January anyway and then we were -- went to cross the Channel on English ships where we got tea and lamb and so on, very wonderful food, but we landed at LeHavre. We got in -- you couldn't dock there. You had to climb down nets into landing craft and be ferried to the shore and then walked seemed like a million miles, get on the French 40 and 8's cars, which we had heard about from World War I and we were quite convinced they were exactly the same cars that had been used in World War I and they shipped us off to a French chateau where we were packed in like sardines and we stayed there for a week or so and then they moved us to an area that was where they had tents. Fortunately they had flush in them and it was a beautiful green field when we arrived and within a half a day it was solid mud about four to six inches deep everywhere and we -- this is where we got replacements for the people that we had lost or for some of the people that we had lost Christmas. And so we got in a lieutenant, one lieutenant he wasn't shipped to the Bulge. He was sick and I forget what was wrong with him, appendicitis or something of that nature and so we lost him in England. And then we got some other replacements for the rest of the people. And I got a couple more people from my squad there and we stayed there for a little while because the most exciting thing that happened there was finally we are issued some live ammunition and we were told under no circumstances are your rifles or fire them for any reason. And I was standing around one day and it sounded like the battle had arrived. It appears that there was a what was claimed to be a wild boar anyway. It may have been a tamed pig that got out, I don't know, but running along the edge of the woods near us and everybody that had a rifle I think shot at the pig and they finally did get the pig, but they didn't get the pig because some Frenchman came along and took the pig away. So we didn't even get the pig, but there was a good deal of chewing of people that had fired their weapons at this and all sorts of threats, but we knew we were going to go into combat very shortly and actually what do you threaten an infantryman with who is about to go into combat anyway.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Won't let you go.

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Wouldn't let us go. That would be terrible. But anyway, they loaded us on our 40 and 8's and we went on up through, up into Belgium. And on our way we got -- we were stopped quite often, pulled off onto sightings for other traffic and during one of those we had an opportunity to see a thousand plane raid go over headed for somewhere in Germany and that was really, really quite a sight. They just kept coming and coming and coming. It was amazing. And we moved up into Belgium and into a town. I don't know where it is, trying to find the places you have been on the map can be a little trying. I have a -- I have been making up a map for our reunion which we are having in June for I have been trying to find places and I found a couple. I got a rather large scale map of Germany and I found a couple that I hadn't found before, but there is still some I can't locate. But anyway, we moved into this town and it had obviously been part of the Battle of the Bulge because there was German and American military equipment. There were mortar shells and machine gun ammunition and everything just scattered all over the place. I don't know whether there had been some collection of things and things had just been dumped there or what. We were quite surprised to see that. I guess maybe we shouldn't have been surprised. And then shortly after that we moved up into what had been the secret line. At that time the front lines were essentially back to where they had been before the Battle of the Bulge right on the border of Germany and Siegfried line and we were in one of the bunkers that had been part of the Siegfried line where we lived while we were waiting to move up into combat and we did a lot of work repairing roads and so on. They were using us for that. And we found we weren't too well fed at that time. They didn't -- there was a break down in the supplies and so we were getting something like one sea ration a day per man and some of the -- somebody managed to kill a deer so we had deer stew for one of our meals that we had and then we were out on the repairing the roads and we found or I found a what had been a dugout from for the Battle of the Bulge and there were some sea rations there and there were some sea rations that were open and partially eaten. So I assumed from that that they had been surprised in the middle of a meal by the Germans coming through there and this is also where we saw our first dead Germans and found one that had not been found by the grave registration there and that was the first actual war time casualty we saw.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What did you think when you saw that?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Well, that's kind of what I expected. Actually the reactions to dead people was interesting from some people. They didn't bother me, but there is some guys particularly after our first attack that there were some dead Germans and they were scared to death to go anywhere near them, particularly at night. But that's the way people react to things differently. But we finally then moved up in our first combat and one of the more intense ones that we were in was taking a little town called Oberreifferscheid and not far from the border of Germany and we being in the mortar section we were among the last ones to move in and we were in a group of trees and there was a rather deep ravine on the right and the town was on the -- to our left front and there was a road down that and there was quite a bit of German artillery fire and we were not very bright at that time. We didn't know anything about being shelled and so on. So we went into the trees so they couldn't see us. Well, that wasn't a good idea because they started firing at the trees. Of course, got tree bursts. Well, we -- one of the fellows was hit, but very fortunately he was one of the other squad leaders and he had on his field jacket and he was wearing an ammunition bag and sweater and about seven other things. So it knocked him down and knocked him unconscious for a minute, but the piece of shrapnel that hit him never got all the way to him. So he was very fortunate in that respect, but we didn't -- my unit of weapons platoon didn't lose anybody that day, but we had fairly heavy casualties in the rifle company that and rifle platoons that took the town and almost got shot by our own people. The company that was beside us our people had gotten into town. They came up and almost started firing on them, but they managed to let them know that they were Americans. So that didn't happen at that time and --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you remember what you were thinking or feeling on that first day of combat?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: I would say feeling well, this is what it is all about. That's about it. I was not particularly frightened. I mean I wasn't too apprehensive at that time. Maybe I should have been more apprehensive than I was, but it is kind of this is what I was more or less prepared for. I mean it was different than what I had imagined it entirely, but it was not too great a shock and I'll admit that I wasn't a really front line individual. We wasn't until later on that I was actually under small arms fire. It was all artillery at that time and artillery is very frightening because you have absolutely no control over that at all. You just have to sit there and hope that you are fortunate. With small arms you maybe feel that you have some control over things, but not much. But we moved up to the what the house that we had as our command post that evening and oh, around midnight or little later, it was very cold and we had left all our packs behind and so we were cold. And we were out in the -- we were out in kind of a shed. The German way the barn is right onto the house. Well, I was out in the barn. But they came in and said, well, there is somebody out here that is calling for help and so our lieutenant that we got in in France and a couple of other people went out to see who that was and before very long why we heard an explosion and one of them came back and said, well, that was -- there is mines out there and the lieutenant got hit. So another guy and I went out and we retrieved the lieutenant and brought him back and didn't see him again for about 50 years. He is now one of the ones that attends our reunions. He was very happy. The first time he came he didn't -- he had a head wound among other things and he didn't have any idea what happened and so he was very happy to find out what had occurred. And but we then set up our mortars, oh, about 50 or 60 yards away and what had been a bunker that the Germans had built there and being used by the other side. We had a son-powered telephone that went out to there and every morning why they'd throw a few rounds of artillery at us and then there was also some heavy machine gun fire, which is where you, I found out the bullets go zing, zing, zing. They go snap, snap, snap when they go by and they the next morning we went out and I helped bring in some of the wounded that had been there and then they shelled us all the way out there to collect them and all the way back, but very fortunately nobody got hit. And it was one of those times that I felt, well, I don't have a thing to worry about. Nothing is going to happen and it didn't. I was fortunate in that respect. But we sat there for about -- I have the date, but it doesn't make any difference, but about a week, something like that and they had then gotten the bridge at Remagen and we didn't know that, but the day before the bridge fell or the day that the bridge fell we heard quite a few trucks and so on over where the Germans were and the next morning we woke up and there were no more Germans there. So they had pulled back all of them that could to get across the Rhine and back into Germany, although we didn't really know that at the time and then we moved from there to a town called Schmidtheim where we sat for about a week and cleaned things up and got re-organized, and finally had sort of a bath after awhile and they then told us that we were going to go up to Duren which was a supply area or had been used as or going to be used as a supply area and that we were going to guard Duren and the supplies were there and we thought, hey, that's all right. We can stand that. And so we got up to Duren and we -- the middle of the city was essentially flat, but the outskirts there was still quite a few usable buildings and we got into what had been an apartment complex. All the tile on the roof was gone, but at least the building was still intact and so I thought, well, if we are going to be here to guard supplies for a while I'll collect some tiles and retile the roof. So I spent most of a day retiling the roof and people wandered around bringing back furniture and so on from the other buildings. I mean there was nobody there. And so we were there about two days and they said, oh, we aren't going to do that after all. And so we went down and crossed the Rhine just below Remagen. The bridge itself had collapsed by that time, excuse me, but they had a pontoon bridge probably more than one, but we crossed on a pontoon bridge across the Rhine that was just south of Remagen and we then went to a town just east of Koblenz and then they said that there was a riot in Wetzlar and so we were sent there to quell the riot. Well, there wasn't much of a riot in Wetzlar when we got there anyway, but there was the Leitz camera factory there and so a couple of people were managed to liberate Leica cameras and so on but --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Is that riot with civilians?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Civilians, yeah, and there also was a large wine seller at Wetzlar and so they were having problems there. So they had a sober spot. I don't drink. I never did drink and so they said, well, anybody that doesn't drink we will appoint you as a sober squad so if the people that are watching the wine seller become incapacitated you can go and take over. Well, we weren't called upon to do that fortunately and we were in a house that was adjacent to a small optical works there and among other things that they did have there was they had a pair of German artillery field glasses with a mill scale in them and so on. So I collected those since they had taken our -- we originally had some 6 by 30 binoculars with a mill scale in them in the United States for squad leaders in mortar sections, but they took those away from us and gave us civilian binoculars which they had collected from people in the United States. And I got a pair of very nice 7 by 50 binoculars, but they had no mill scale in them which is a very -- a help if you are going to be firing a mortar to be able to have a mill scale to read how much you have to move your deflection. And so I collected those and I still had the others as well. When I put those in my bedroll at that particular time and a little bit later on why somebody else borrowed them from me permanently. So I didn't get those. I still have the 7 by 50 binoculars without the mill scale, but wait for the cuckoo clock is done. And we then moved on from Wetzlar up to Kassel and there we actually got a shower in Kassel, but these areas had all been taken before this time. But we were in Kassel for a little while and then they said that we were going to get back into actual combat again and so we moved east from Kassel on in trucks, walking, part of the time on tanks, part of the time on armored cars, part of the time with the cannon company vehicles. But we went east from there going through little towns and most of them had lots of white bed sheets out of the windows, but occasionally we would hit some pockets of resistance. Usually they didn't last a real long time and only one time did I actually get to fire my mortar in combat and they had a fairly -- they had a machine gun nest and some other things outside of one town and they actually got people pinned down outside of town and we set up the mortar and fired on the machine gun nest and got them, but that was really the only time I fired my mortar in anger and I got -- we had some small-arms fire that I encountered along the way, but it was really relatively easy most of the way across there. And one of the officers who is our executive officer at that time stayed in the Army and has come to our Company I reunions and he said that at the present time they are using the 69th and the 9th Armored as an illustration of how the infantry and the armour work together to move rapidly across the area and how well this worked. Well, it worked pretty well except most -- at least a good part of the time we were out ahead of the armour when the armour was supposed to be ahead of us and they'd come up to us and what in the world are you doing here? We are supposed to be out there. Well, so things don't always work the way that they are supposed to or they even say they do in wartime. But our final objective was Leipzig and when we got close to Leipzig then we ran into considerably more resistance and we had one town, it wasn't really much of a town, that was quite heavily defended and that was the morning that I woke up and I decided, well, today is the day I'm going to get killed and I was just positive that was going to happen, but fortunately, it did not. But it was not too good a feeling.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What do you think made you feel that way on that day?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: I don't really know. I mean it is we had hit a little bit more resistance than we had for a while, but that -- I was just walking along the road and suddenly that's what I thought. But no, we came under some rather heavy sniper fire there and had a fair problem, had two or three people killed for in our company and so it was -- and there had been fairly strong resistance that some of the other units had encountered the day before. We kind of took which company was lead company, kind of changed from day-to-day and the company that had been lead the day before had encountered quite a bit of resistance. And then we went through there and we were going to be attacking Leipzig and we were coming in from the south of Leipzig and we were going to have a night attack on the city. So we were all told be very -- get everything tight so you don't make noise and so on and we will be moving out. So we moved out and we came to this big open field and we were going across this field and German machine gun opened up in front of us and you can see the -- they were traversing back and forth. You could see the faces come over. There was just a nice pattern of Z's as they moved along except that they were shooting about 20 feet over our heads which was very nice because if they had been shooting 20 feet lower they would have gotten a lot of people, but some -- one of the units that we had with us at that time was a unit of black soldiers who had volunteered to be infantryman They wanted to be infantryman and they were given the name of J Platoon and they were very good and I think that they were the ones that they sent out to take care of that machine gun nest and they did and --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you think they were shooting over you on purpose or were they bad shots?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: I think that they were just bad shots. I think that they were set up poorly and actually they fired a mortar flare and of course, we all hit the ground when that flare went off, but they didn't change anything after the flare. So we were very, very fortunate. It may have been that they were actually set up in a position that they couldn't depress their gun far enough to get to where we were because there were some ridges, couldn't see much at night, but I think there is some sides of the field were higher than others and it may have been they just couldn't get down there. And so we -- we shortly after that we heard a siren which we were later told was the signal that the city of Leipzig had been taken and they had surrendered and so we moved on through Leipzig. We walked through Leipzig and some cars were commandeered to carry people and so on and went on up just north of Leipzig to the Mulde River, which is where we were supposed to stop. The Elbe was part of where they stopped, but all of our units were on the Mulde, which is actually further west than the Elbe. The Elbe runs through Dresden and the Mulde is only, oh, probably 10 or 15 kilometers outside of Leipzig east and so we were in this little town and just set up our mortars there and stayed there and all we were there for was to just keep German soldiers from coming back that way as far as we were concerned. We were not to do any offensive action at all and just sit there. - - - (END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE.) - - - And so we stayed there until about May 2nd, 3rd or 4th, something like that. Then we moved to another town further south still on the Mulde and there there was a bridge and my job there was I was to go across the bridge and there was a railroad line on the other side and I was supposed to parole that railroad line to keep any Germans from fleeing back across the river. Well, I walked probably about three miles and I was supposed to meet a guy that was coming from another direction and when I met him why I would turn around and walk back and as far as I was concerned they could have run the whole German Army across behind me or in front of me and I wouldn't have known anything about it, but that's what I was doing until May 8th when the war was over. Of course, we had heard of Hitler's demise shortly before that and we then, this, of course, was what was going to be the German zone of occupation. We moved back then after the war was over to a town which was actually west of Leipzig, but still in what was going to be the Russian zone and stayed there for oh, several weeks and we were doing a little bit the same things the Russians were. We were going out and collecting any machinery and so on to ship to us and the Russians were shipping everything back to Russia, but I think we were getting it mainly to keep the Russians from getting it when they did take over. But we stayed there and then we are finally shipped back further into Germany in what was eventually the American zone.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you remember any big celebrations on VE day?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: No, there were no great celebration. I mean we were all very happy, but it was -- it was no surprise, let's put it this way. We were -- we were -- we were happy we weren't being shot at and weren't going to be shot at any more, but really nothing had been going on and it was pretty apparent that that there was not going to be any more hostilities well before the official day.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: You have any close buddies in your outfit?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Yeah, one, probably the other one that became the mortar section sergeant was a real good friend of mine, Harris Timmer, who lives up in Michigan now and he is one of the ones who attends our reunions, but I really did not keep in close contact with them after the war was over. We were, I think we were all so busy catching up and doing our things that it wasn't too important. I mentioned that I have a reunion with my, some of the ones from the company, but that first of those reunions we had were about 11 years ago. Now there is a division association and they have had reunions essentially since the time that the war was over. Most of the time I was out in, for a long time anyway I was out in North Dakota, South Dakota, Wisconsin area and that was too far for me to go. Plus, I didn't really have the time or the money to go to things like that. And so it wasn't until about ten years ago, 11 years ago that we started these reunions of the ones that we could locate from Company I.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any close buddies during the war?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: No, I didn't lose any real close ones. I mean the mortar section was very fortunate. We did not have any combat casualties. We had some people that we lost through sickness. The one of my good friends was became sick, one of the other squad leaders and went back to the hospital and that's the last we saw of him. I heard from him once after the war so I know that he came through all right. But I didn't keep in real close contact with any of them after the -- after the war was over.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you have memories of mail call?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah. Mail call was always nice and we got cookies from home, which we, of course, shared around.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Were you able to write much back home?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Well, the reason why I'm able to tell you what we did as well as I did is that immediately after the war was over while we were in this first town near Leipzig, I wrote to my parents some of my war experiences and since those then I have amplified those a little bit and actually I have a book which I wrote and bound and one of my friends, one of the other squad leaders, name is Swanberg, illustrated it for me. It is -- I wrote it after we are having our reunions and he had illustrated our original company history, which was written while we were in that same area. And so I have had a record of a lot of the things that happened, while a lot of the fellows they can't remember, which I think is true because if I hadn't written it down I don't think I would remember that much any more.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: You still have the original letters that you wrote back to your parents?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: That's great.

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Yeah, and as I said, I transcribed them into the book and then I added what happened that was strict to the combat and I added what happened to me in the Army before then and then after the war was over the various places I was in Germany and I actually ended up in Berlin with the 78th Division and was there until just before I was discharged which was interesting.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What happened in those occupation days?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Well, after the war was over we were in Germany and we were all being trained for the Asian Theater. We were going to go over and invade Japan. We were told that we would be sent back to the states and we would be put in sealed troop trains taken to the west coast and get on troop ships and head for the Pacific. We would be taking part in the invasion of Japan. So you can imagine that we were not the least bit unhappy to hear that the atomic bombs had been dropped and that the Japanese had surrendered. Because I mean we were taking classes every day on the Japanese Army, weapons tactics and so on and so we were very pleased that had happened. Well, most of us did not have enough points. The points being you got so much, a point for every year, every month you were in the Army. Two points if you, the month was overseas. You got five points for a Combat Infantryman Badge. I think you got five points for a Bronze Star or something like that and the number of points that you ended up with determined when you were going to go home. Well, we didn't have enough points. And so what essentially happened was that the 69th Division went home, but it wasn't the 69th Division it was the 29th Division because they filled the unit up with people from the 29th Division, all of which had enough points to go home and they went home as the 69th Division and we were primarily partialed out to ordnance companies. I guess there were a lot of ordnance companies. So there are lots of places for people. We didn't do anything when we went to the ordnance companies because there wasn't anything to do. But I was in two different ordnance companies. One was a medium maintenance company and we used a whole bunch of half tracks that were going to be given to the French government and parked them out in the field and I was in another ordnance company that was a small arms maintenance and repair company and we didn't do any of the maintenance or repair. I met a buddy there who had been in the 69th Division Cannon Company and we had ridden on the truck with him one time and he was kind of a wheeler dealer and he liked me, I guess. So he and I ran the beer haul and I don't drink, so I guess I was a good candidate for that, but we ran the beer haul there and we finally ended up near, between Bremen and Bremerhaven. On the other side of the river, a little town called Brakel and then in November of 1945 I was transferred to the 29th Division in Berlin and I was there and I had Thanksgiving dinner and they said that they were going home and I didn't have enough points. So I was then sent to the 78th Division in Berlin. And as I said, I was in Berlin until I came home. When you were in Berlin you had to wait until you had a replacement before you came home as well as having the right number of points. And so I was there until April of 1946 and I, after I came home and was home for a while I thought, well, gee, I should have seen more of Berlin than I did there. There was lots of things should have been to see in Berlin. I saw the Brandenburg Gate and I saw the Reich Chancellery and so on. Those were in the Russian zone. And we weren't encouraged to go into the Russian zone at all. You always went in at least two's and you didn't go at night under any circumstances because relations were not too great even at that time between the Russians and the Americans, but I was back to Berlin about three years ago and I realized why I didn't see anything because there was nothing to see at that time. Everything was either bombed out or completely closed down. I mean museums, things of that nature and so I saw the sights of Berlin a little bit later, but there really wasn't much to see. It was quite interesting, the Tear Garden, the big park just outside the Brandenburg Gate, when I was there was just absolutely flat. There wasn't a tree in sight. They all had either been blown or they had all been burned for firewood is what happened to all the trees and there are all trees there. They are all 50 years old and very nice trees but --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you finally did get back home?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Oh, very good, very good. Got home on Easter Sunday and very -- I was very happy to get home. I got home at a good time. I remember I was very -- I was planning to continue my education, also. And it wasn't too long until I could go to summer school and there was a small college in the town where I lived, so I went there. And of course, I had the GI bill which I was very grateful for. I would have got an education anyway, but it made it much easier and really helped me in getting my advanced degrees.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Backtracking a bit, did you have much contact with the German people when you were in Germany during the war?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Some. Not -- not any close contact. Of course, the main contact that we had with them was throwing them out of their house so that we could be in their house and we were not very polite about that. I will be very honest. I will say this, I felt that the German people were quite a lot like the American people seeing their houses and so on. They like gadgets. We like gadgets. They were quite modern in their indoor plumbing, so on. I mean it was not -- it was different than the U.S., but you could see the similarities between the two. Then, of course, after the war for a long time we had the non-fraternization rule and I was a good person and I did not fraternize but --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: But some did probably, right?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Oh, yes, there was a lot of fraternization. Now, we -- when we were running our beer haul up in Brakel we did have some contact. We hired a German band that came in and we could collect the band and bring them in and have them play for us and my friend, the other guy is that ran the beer haul with me, spoke a little German and I got to the point with my German where I was either got just exactly what they were saying or I thought they were saying exactly the opposite of it, one of the two, but we -- we talked with members of the band quite a bit. Some of them had been in the German Army, of course. Of course, they were all on the eastern front. Everybody had been on the eastern front.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you have any contacts, much contact with the French people when you were there?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Very, very little and what we had was not particularly good. We were not in France too much, but I mean the difference between France and Belgium was like night and day as far as I was concerned. France was dirty and in Belgium although the war had gone through there things were clean and neat and so on. It was -- it was a tremendous difference that I noticed on those two. I did -- I had zero contact with the Belgian people. I did not see a single Belgian person. All I saw was the countryside as compared with France. In France we had very, very little contact with the people.Thomas A. Swope:: How about the British people when you were there?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Oh, they were very, very, very nice. They had their equivalent of the U.S.O. and Red Cross clubs and we went to a few of those and got TIO. We felt a little guilty about doing that because they didn't have nearly as much as we did. We did do that occasionally and they organized a dance for us in this little town where we were and the relationships as far as I was concerned between Americans and the British people was -- were very good and I did get up to London and saw some of the sights of London at that time.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you get any shows when you were in France or Germany, U.S.O. shows or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Nope. We saw one, one Red Cross doughnut wagon someplace and I think they got lost is how they happened to see us. But no, after the war was over I was able and one of the ordnance companies, I think, I was able to go to see Bob Hope at one of the airbases. And we were trucked over there. I did get to go and see a, I think it was a ballet in Leipzig while I was there. That was one of the things that we could do from where we were. But I mean that was -- that was German entertainment, that was not U.S.O. or anything of that nature.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything about the Bob Hope show?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Oh, yeah, not -- not in great detail, but Bob Hope and Jerry Colonna were the ones I remember the most on that. I couldn't tell you any jokes.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: He probably used the same jokes.

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: I'm sure he did.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: When you think about your experiences during the war, does one specific vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Well, I think probably the most vivid memories are our first day in combat, the being in the forest and the artillery fire there and going out and getting the wounded that night are probably, that and then as I said, the day that I thought I was going to be killed, the subsequent events of that probably are as stand out as much as anything. Also, in this little town on the Mulde River I can remember we had a -- there was a barn out behind the house there that overlooked the river and we went out there, the upper part of it, removed a tile so we could lookout and see as an observation post and one morning there was an ME-110 German airplane that flew right over us and that was the last German aircraft I saw and it was fairly low. I was wondering where he thinks he is going.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Well, very good. You think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Robert M. McMillan
sp.p: Oh, I think so. [Interview ends]
